threads.thread_goal: Align on incident scenarios, scope, and playbook structure.

messages.text: Kicking off the work on our Crisis Communication Playbook for On-site Security Incidents (project_title: Crisis Communication Playbook for On‑Site Security Incidents). Goal for this thread: align on which incident scenarios we cover in v1 and the overall structure/owners for the playbook.  To get us started, I suggest we use T1 and T2 as our anchors:  - T1: map typical on-site security incident scenarios and current response gaps  - T2: draft the playbook structure and ownership matrix  We also have A8 (Stakeholder and Contact Matrix) as a backbone for who needs to be in the loop.  Proposal for initial incident types, based on past drills and common patterns:  1) Unauthorised person on site / trespass  2) Physical altercation or threat against staff  3) Fire or suspected fire  4) Suspicious package or bomb threat  5) Medical emergency on site  6) Major facility disruption (power outage, structural issue)  Can you react in this thread with any missing scenarios or ones that feel less relevant for v1? Once we agree on 4–6, we can lock them in and move to the table of contents and section owners.

Thanks for framing this. From a media and public-facing angle, those six cover most of what tends to attract attention. If we need to trim to 5 for v1, I would consider grouping suspicious package and bomb threat under one heading, since the communication logic is similar.  One thing I do not see explicitly is an incident involving law enforcement activity on site (for example, police search or arrest). That can be very sensitive for both staff and community. It might fit under unauthorised person, but I would call it out so we do not miss specific constraints.  For T1, I can help document how these are currently handled from the perspective of external communication and where we see gaps, then sync with a security guard representative for validation.

From what I have seen on site, these are the ones that really throw people off:  - Fights or threats between visitors or against staff  - Fire alarms going off, especially when we are not sure if it is real  - Suspicious bags or boxes left in odd places  - Medical issues where someone collapses or is unresponsive  Power cuts are stressful but usually operations handles them more than security.  For law enforcement on site, that does happen and it changes how much we can say. I would keep that separate from a random trespasser.  For T1, I can write out the current steps guards usually take for each of these, including who we call first and what we say on the radio. It might not be pretty, but it will show the gaps.

Agree that we should keep the list tight for v1 so the playbook is usable under pressure. Building on what you all shared, I would suggest we define scenarios in a way that maps cleanly to communication flows. For example:  1) Safety threat involving people (altercation, violent threat, law enforcement action)  2) Fire or smoke event  3) Suspicious object or bomb threat  4) Medical emergency  5) Site infrastructure disruption (power, structural, major system failure)  That gives us five buckets. Within each, we can note sub-variants. For T2, this structure would make it easier to assign owners per phase: detect, verify, escalate, internal updates, external updates, and recovery.  If we agree on these five, we can lock them as the v1 scope and still note that we will revisit after the first drill.

From a training and comprehension angle, I like the idea of five clear buckets, as long as the names are intuitive for guards and front-line staff. We can always show examples under each.  I would slightly rephrase to match how people talk on site:  1) Violence or threat to people (including police activity)  2) Fire or smoke  3) Suspicious item or bomb threat  4) Medical emergency  5) Major building problem (power, structure, systems)  For T2, this also helps me later when we design the internal briefing templates and training (T5 and T6) so that the same wording appears everywhere.  If no one objects, I suggest we confirm these five as the v1 scenarios and move on to the table of contents and owners.

No objection from my side. Summarising what I am hearing so we can close the scope for v1:  - We will cover five priority scenarios:  1) Violence or threat to people (including law enforcement activity)  2) Fire or smoke  3) Suspicious item or bomb threat  4) Medical emergency  5) Major building problem (power, structure, systems)  - Law enforcement on site is explicitly called out under the first scenario.  - Power and structural issues are grouped under major building problem.  Unless anyone flags a strong concern today, I suggest we treat this as our agreed list for v1 and capture it under T1. That will let us move on to the playbook structure and ownership matrix in T2.

Works for me. Moving to structure, here is a draft table of contents for A1 (Crisis Communication Playbook v1.0) that we can refine:  1. Purpose, scope, and principles  2. Roles and contacts overview (link to A8)  3. Common communication rules (tone, languages, do and do not)  4. Scenario playbooks (one per scenario, each with phases)     4.1 Violence or threat to people     4.2 Fire or smoke     4.3 Suspicious item or bomb threat     4.4 Medical emergency     4.5 Major building problem  5. Media and external communication basics (link to A3 and A5)  6. Internal staff updates and briefings (link to A4)  7. Training, drills, and review (link to A6 and A7)  For T2, we also need an ownership matrix. I can draft a RACI proposal, but I would like input on who should be accountable per section.

I like this structure; it is easy to navigate. For the ownership matrix in T2, here is a first pass on who leads each section, assuming we keep sign-offs with legal and operations outside this group:  1. Purpose, scope, principles – owned by 409854  2. Roles and contacts overview (A8) – co-owned by 409854 with input from operations  3. Common communication rules – 143124 as lead, since this ties closely to media practice  4. Scenario playbooks – shared:      - Violence or threat to people – 47290 and 286680      - Fire or smoke – 47290 with operations input      - Suspicious item or bomb threat – 47290 with operations input      - Medical emergency – 47290 with HR or health and safety input      - Major building problem – 286680 with operations input  5. Media and external communication basics (A3, A5) – 143124  6. Internal staff updates and briefings (A4) – 47537  7. Training, drills, and review (A6, A7) – 47537 with support from 409854  Open to adjustments, but this gives us a concrete starting point for T2.

I can take the lead on the parts that are closest to what guards actually do:  - Violence or threat to people  - Fire or smoke  - Suspicious item or bomb threat  - Medical emergency  For major building problems, I can add what we see on the ground, but operations will know more about systems.  I will need some help turning my notes into clean wording for A1, but I can at least get the steps and who we call into T1 and then into the scenario sections.

Happy to own section 6 (internal staff updates and briefings) and co-own section 7 on training and drills. That lines up with T5, T6, and T9. I will make sure the language is simple and consistent with the scenario names we agreed.  For the RACI in T2, I suggest we keep it light: one clear owner per section, plus a note that legal and operations must sign off on anything that touches regulations or safety procedures.

Let me capture the ownership proposal so we can confirm it for T2:  - Section 1 (Purpose, scope, principles): 409854  - Section 2 (Roles and contacts, A8): 409854 with operations  - Section 3 (Common rules): 143124  - Section 4 (Scenarios):     4.1 Violence or threat to people – 47290 and 286680     4.2 Fire or smoke – 47290     4.3 Suspicious item or bomb threat – 47290     4.4 Medical emergency – 47290     4.5 Major building problem – 286680  - Section 5 (Media and external basics, A3, A5): 143124  - Section 6 (Internal updates, A4): 47537  - Section 7 (Training, drills, review, A6, A7): 47537 with support from 409854  If everyone is comfortable with this, we can treat the structure and owners as agreed and move ahead with drafting under T2.

This breakdown works for me. It gives clear leads while still allowing for cross-checks. I will take ownership of section 3 and 5 and make sure they align with our media practice and regulatory constraints, then route them to legal for review.  From my side, we can mark the table of contents and section owners as agreed for T2, unless someone sees a gap.

All good from my side as well. Having this structure now will make it easier to design the training flow later so that staff see the same sections in A1, in the briefings (A4), and in the drills (A6).  I suggest we formally confirm this structure and ownership matrix so we can move into drafting.

Great, thanks all. To close this out:  - We have agreed on five priority scenarios for v1, as listed earlier.  - We have agreed on the overall table of contents for A1 and the section owners as summarised in M11.  I will document this under T2 and share a first draft of the playbook skeleton so everyone can start filling in their parts.

threads.thread_goal: Define on-site escalation scripts and quick-reference checklists.

messages.text: I have put together a first rough draft of the on-site incident reporting and escalation script based on what guards actually do today, mapped to the five scenarios we agreed. This is meant to feed into T3 and T8 and eventually into A2.  For each scenario, I wrote:  - What the guard should say on the radio first  - Who they call next (control room, site manager, emergency services)  - What information they must confirm before escalating  Example for violence or threat to people:  1) Radio: 'Control, this is [name] at [location]. I have a violent incident in progress. One person with [weapon/no weapon], number of people involved [x]. Request immediate support.'  2) Move people away if safe, do not try to be a hero.  3) Call emergency services if there is a weapon or serious injury.  I know the wording needs to be cleaned up and checked by legal and safety. Can you review and tell me what is missing or confusing before we turn this into the final A2 checklist?

Thanks for drafting this. The structure makes sense and feels close to how people actually talk on the radio, which is good. A few questions so we can make it checklist-ready for A2:  - Do you use any standard code words or signal phrases on the radio that we should keep, or is plain language preferred?  - For each scenario, can we add a simple 'do not' list (for example, do not share names over the radio, do not speculate on causes)?  - For escalation, it might help to show a simple path: Guard -> Control room -> Site manager -> Communications contact (from A8).  Once we clarify these, I can help turn your script into a one-page checklist per scenario under T8.

On the radio we mostly use plain language. Some sites have codes, but they are not the same everywhere, so I would not put codes in A2. We can add a note that local codes can be added at site level.  For 'do not', I can list what usually causes trouble:  - Do not say names or ID numbers on open channels  - Do not say what you think happened, only what you see  - Do not promise anything to bystanders  For escalation, yes, the path you wrote matches what we try to do. I will add a simple line for each scenario: 'After first radio call, inform control room, then site manager, then communications contact from A8 if needed.'

I read through your draft with the training lens on. It is very practical, which is great. To make it easier to remember under stress, I suggest we use the same pattern for all five scenarios:  1) See it – what you check first  2) Say it – exact radio phrase  3) Send it – who you escalate to, in order  4) Secure – what you do to keep people safe while waiting  5) Share – what you log or report after  If you are ok with that, I can help reformat your text into that pattern for T3 and then we can mirror it in the training materials (T6) so guards practice the same steps.

From a media and external perspective, the key is that nothing in the on-site script conflicts with what we can say publicly later. A few points to watch:  - Avoid any language that sounds like assigning blame or confirming causes.  - Make sure there is a clear step where the communications contact is informed early enough, using A8.  - For incidents likely to attract attention (violence, fire, suspicious item), we should add a simple note: 'Do not speak to media or post on social media. Direct all questions to the designated spokesperson.'  Once you and 47537 stabilise the wording for T3, I can do a quick pass to check for any red flags before we call A2 final.

I like the 'See it, Say it, Send it, Secure, Share' pattern. It is easy to remember. I can rework my draft into that order for each scenario.  For example, for suspicious item:  - See it: do not touch, check if anyone is nearby, note exact location  - Say it: radio control with location and what you see, not what you think it is  - Send it: control room, site manager, then follow their instructions about police or bomb squad  - Secure: move people away calmly, keep exits clear  - Share: write down time, what you saw, who you informed  I will update the rest of the scenarios like this and share a cleaned-up version for T3.

That example reads very clearly. Once you have the full set in the new pattern, I can turn each scenario into a one-page checklist for T8:  - Top section: See it / Say it / Send it / Secure / Share  - Bottom section: 'Do not' list and escalation path with references to A8  I will also check that the layout works both for print and for mobile screenshots, since guards may use either. Before we call A2 final, we should test at least one scenario with two guards to see if anything is confusing.

Once the checklists are drafted under T8, I can run a short tabletop exercise with a small group of guards to test clarity, as part of the prep for T6. We can pick two scenarios, walk through them step by step, and capture any feedback before we freeze A2.  For availability on site, my suggestion is that we use both printed copies in key locations and a digital version accessible on phones, but we should confirm what is realistic for each site.

Catching up on this thread. The pattern you have landed on is strong and consistent, and the focus on plain language fits our constraint that materials must be usable under stress.  On availability: from past projects, relying only on digital access can be risky during power or network issues. I would recommend we explicitly decide that A2 will be available both as printed one-pagers in guard rooms and as digital files that can be shared to phones. We can then ask operations to handle local printing and placement.  If you agree, we can record that as our approach for T8.

Agree on using both print and digital for A2. That also helps us keep a consistent version while allowing sites to place the checklists where they make most sense. We just need to make sure version control is clear so old printouts are replaced when we update.  On the content itself, once 47290 and 47537 are happy with the wording for T3, please send it my way and I will do a quick review for any phrasing that could create issues if repeated outside the site. After that, I think we can call the escalation checklist final for v1.

I will finish reworking the scripts into the See/Say/Send/Secure/Share pattern today and share them in a doc for T3. After your review, we can freeze the wording for v1.  From my side, the approach of having both printed and digital A2 checklists works well. Guards like having something on the wall, but also on their phones.

To wrap this up, here is how I see the path:  - 47290 finalises the scenario scripts for T3 using the agreed pattern.  - 143124 reviews for any sensitive phrasing.  - I convert them into one-page checklists per scenario for T8, designed for both print and mobile.  - 47537 tests two scenarios with guards and collects feedback.  If no major issues come up, we can treat A2 as the approved escalation checklist for v1.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on media holding statements, Q&A, and channel strategy.

messages.text: I have drafted initial media holding statements and a basic channel mapping for our five scenarios, to move T4 and T7 forward and start shaping A3 and A5.  For each scenario, A3 currently includes:  - One short holding statement (what we can say in the first 30–60 minutes)  - A few key facts we can confirm early  - A list of what we will not comment on yet  For example, for violence or threat to people:  - Holding statement: 'We are aware of an incident involving a threat to personal safety at our [location] site. Our priority is the safety of our staff, visitors, and the surrounding community. We are working closely with the authorities and will provide further information as soon as we can.'  For A5, the draft channel strategy for this scenario is:  - Internal: email to staff plus message via internal chat if available  - External: short web update and prepared lines for media calls  - Social: only if there is visible impact or media coverage, with approval from legal and senior management  Please review tone, clarity, and any missing constraints before we refine and select the default statements per scenario.

Thanks for sharing this. The example statement reads balanced and should be understandable to non-specialists, which is key. A few suggestions before we lock anything in A3:  - For incidents involving law enforcement, we may want a variant that explicitly notes we are cooperating fully, without implying any outcome.  - For medical emergencies, we should be very careful not to disclose personal details or speculate on condition.  On A5, I would like us to define a simple severity scale (for example, low, medium, high impact) and map channels to that, so we do not over-communicate small incidents or under-communicate major ones. That will also help operations know when to loop us in.

From the internal side, the tone of your example works well. It is calm, factual, and avoids blame. For A3, I would suggest we add one or two internal-only key messages per scenario that managers can use when talking to their teams, so they do not improvise.  For A5, I like the idea of a simple severity scale. It will also help us align internal briefings (A4) with external messages so staff do not hear something different from what we say publicly.

Looking at this from the spokesperson angle, the holding statement you shared is something I would feel comfortable saying on camera. It is short enough to remember and covers the basics.  For A3, I would propose that for each scenario we pick one default holding statement that works across channels (press, web, social), and then we can have a few optional lines for specific questions. That will make it easier for spokespeople to stay consistent.  On A5, I agree we should define who approves what: for example, internal notes by 409854 or 47537, external statements by 143124 with legal sign-off, and social posts only after senior management approval.

From the site side, the wording sounds fine, but I want to flag that guards will sometimes be asked by people on the ground what is happening before any official statement is out. It would help if A3 also had one or two simple lines we can use on site, like: 'There is an incident and we are following our safety procedures. Please move to [location] and wait for further instructions.'  That way we do not say something that conflicts with the official message later.

Good point. I will add a short 'on-site line' for each scenario in A3, focused on safety instructions and not on causes. That should help guards and front-line staff stay aligned with the external message.  On the severity scale for A5, here is a simple proposal:  - Level 1 (low): contained incident, no injuries, limited impact. Internal note only, no external statement.  - Level 2 (medium): visible impact on operations or community interest likely. Internal note plus web update if needed.  - Level 3 (high): serious injury, major disruption, or heavy media interest. Full internal and external activation, including web, media, and possibly social.  We can then map each scenario to typical levels and channels in T7.

I like this three-level model. It is simple enough to remember and gives us a clear way to decide when to go public. For T7, we should also specify who decides the level in real time. My suggestion:  - Initial level proposed by the on-call operations manager.  - Confirmed by the communications lead on duty (from A8).  That way we avoid over-escalation based on incomplete information.  On A3, I support the idea of one default holding statement per scenario, with optional add-ons for specific questions.

For internal alignment, it would help if the severity level also appears in the internal briefings (A4) so staff understand why they are seeing more or less information. For example, 'This is a level 2 incident, which means...' with a short explanation.  Once you finalise the default holding statements in A3, I can mirror the key points in the internal templates so managers do not improvise their own versions.

To move towards a decision on the default holding statements, could you share a quick summary of the options per scenario and which one you recommend as the primary? That will make it easier for us to react and confirm.  For example:  - Violence or threat: Option A (what you shared), Option B (shorter), recommended: A.  Once we agree on one per scenario, we can mark them as the default in A3 and use them as the base for media training.

Sure, here is a condensed view of the options and my recommendation for each scenario in A3:  - Violence or threat: Option A (longer, more context), Option B (shorter). I recommend Option B: 'We are managing an incident involving a threat to personal safety at our [location] site. Our priority is the safety of everyone on site and the surrounding community. We are working with the authorities and will share more information when we can.'  - Fire or smoke: Option C (mentions fire services), Option D (more generic). I recommend C, as it reassures that professionals are involved.  - Suspicious item or bomb threat: Option E (very cautious), Option F (more detail). I recommend E to avoid speculation.  - Medical emergency: Option G (focus on individual), Option H (focus on process). I recommend H to avoid personal details.  - Major building problem: Option I (mentions cause), Option J (focus on impact). I recommend J to avoid guessing causes.  If you are comfortable with these, we can mark them as the default holding statements in A3.

These recommendations make sense to me and align with our need to avoid speculation and protect privacy. I support marking these as the default holding statements for v1 in A3. We can always refine after the first drill or real incident.  On A5 and T7, I also support the three-level severity model and the approval flow you outlined earlier. If no one objects, we can confirm both the default statements and the multi-channel strategy as our baseline.

I am aligned as well. The recommended options are all statements I would be comfortable delivering in a press briefing or short interview. Having one default per scenario in A3 will also simplify training.  For A5, the three-level model plus clear approval flow (operations proposes level, communications confirms, legal signs off on external statements, senior management approves social for level 3) gives us enough structure without slowing us down too much.

No objections from me. Once you lock these defaults into A3, I will update the internal briefing templates (A4) so that managers see the same core messages, adapted for staff. I will also reference the severity levels so they can explain why we are communicating in a certain way.

Great, thanks all. To summarise and close this thread:  - We have selected one default holding statement per scenario in A3, based on the recommendations in M36.  - We have agreed on a three-level severity model and mapped channels and approvals in A5: internal only for level 1, internal plus web for level 2 when needed, and full internal and external activation for level 3, with legal and senior management sign-off where required.  I will update A3 and A5 accordingly under T4 and T7 and share the updated versions for final legal review.

threads.thread_goal: Finalize internal briefing templates and training approach.

messages.text: I have prepared first drafts of the internal staff briefing templates and the training session outline to move T5, T6, and T9 forward and to start shaping A4 and A6.  For A4 (Internal Staff Briefing Templates), I created:  - A short email template for initial incident notification  - A follow-up template for when more facts are available  - A post-incident update template  Each uses simple language, references the severity level from A5, and includes three parts: what happened, what we are doing, what staff should do or not do.  For T6, the training session plan is a 60-minute session:  - 10 min: why we have a playbook  - 20 min: walk-through of the five scenarios and the See/Say/Send/Secure/Share pattern  - 20 min: two short tabletop exercises using A2 and A4  - 10 min: Q and A  For T9 and A6, I drafted a basic drill plan and evaluation form that we can adapt per site.  Please review tone, structure, and timing, and let me know what feels off or missing before we finalise.

Thanks for pulling this together. The structure looks solid and the 60-minute plan fits our constraint. A few comments:  - On A4, I like the three-part structure. Could we add a short line in each template reminding staff not to share unverified information on social media?  - For the training (T6), we should make sure at least one session per site includes someone from communications or operations, so questions about escalation and approvals can be answered on the spot.  - For A6 and T9, it would help to include a simple rating scale in the evaluation form (for example, clarity of roles, clarity of messages, ease of using A2 and A4).

I went through the templates in A4. The tone is clear and neutral, which is what we want. A couple of tweaks from the external communications side:  - For initial notifications, avoid giving numbers of injured or affected people unless confirmed and cleared by legal. Maybe use 'a number of people' until we know more.  - For post-incident updates, it would be good to include a short line about how we will capture lessons learned, linking to A7.  On the training (T6), I can join at least one dry run to make sure the way we explain media and social media constraints is consistent with A3 and A5.

From a guard perspective, the templates are easy to read. I like that they say clearly what staff should do or not do. One suggestion: in the initial notification, can we add a simple line like 'Security and site management are handling the situation' so people know someone is in charge?  For the training, it would help if we can show a real example of A2 and A4 on screen and maybe give printed copies, so people see what they will actually use.

The 60-minute structure looks workable. From experience, the tabletop exercises are where people really internalise the steps, so I would suggest we keep at least 20 minutes for them, as you planned.  For A6 and T9, maybe we can define two standard drill scenarios for v1 (for example, violence or threat, and fire or smoke) so we can compare results across sites. We can always add more later, but starting with two will make evaluation easier.

Thanks for the feedback. I will:  - Add a short reminder in each A4 template about not sharing unverified information on social media.  - Update the evaluation form in A6 to include a simple 1–5 rating for clarity of roles, clarity of messages, and ease of using A2 and A4.  For T6, I will note that each site should have at least one session with a communications or operations representative present to handle escalation questions.

Good points on numbers and lessons learned. I will adjust the A4 templates so that:  - Initial notifications use cautious wording about numbers until confirmed.  - Post-incident updates include a short line about the review process, with a reference to A7.  For the training dry run under T6, I would appreciate your presence to cover questions about media and social media boundaries.

I will add that line about security and site management handling the situation into the initial notification template. It should help reassure staff.  In the training session (T6), we will definitely show real examples of A2 and A4 on screen and provide printed copies where possible, so people can follow along and mark them up if needed.

I like the idea of standardising on two core drill scenarios for v1. Violence or threat and fire or smoke are good choices, as they cover very different dynamics. We can note in A6 and T9 that sites may add more scenarios later, but these two should be run at least once per year.  On the training format, are we comfortable saying that the default is live sessions, with recordings used as a backup for night shifts or remote staff?

Live sessions as the default make sense to me, especially for the tabletop parts. Recordings can work for awareness, but they do not replace practice. I would frame it as a mixed approach:  - Live 60-minute sessions as the standard.  - Recorded overview plus short refreshers for those who cannot attend live.  That way we set expectations but still give flexibility.

I agree with a mixed approach. For T6, I will document that:  - The primary format is a live 60-minute session with exercises.  - We will also provide a recorded overview and short refresher clips for those who cannot attend live or for later refreshers.  For A6 and T9, I will set violence or threat and fire or smoke as the two standard drill scenarios for v1, with an option for sites to add more once they are comfortable.

From my side, the updated A4 templates and the training approach you described sound aligned with the external messaging we defined in A3 and A5. As long as we keep the cautions about numbers and causes, I am comfortable with managers using these templates without additional review in most cases.  For very sensitive incidents, we can always ask that internal messages be checked by communications before sending, but that can be handled in the playbook text rather than in the templates themselves.

Given the feedback, I propose we formally confirm two points:  1) The internal staff briefing templates in A4, with the adjustments discussed, are approved for v1.  2) The training format for T6 will be a mixed model: live 60-minute sessions as the default, supported by recorded overviews and refreshers, with two standard drill scenarios (violence or threat, and fire or smoke) defined in A6 and T9.  If there are no objections, we can record these as our decisions and move on to scheduling.
No objections from me. I will treat the current A4 templates as final for v1 and update the training and drill documentation to reflect the mixed format and the two standard scenarios.

threads.thread_goal: Close out project with review process and distribution plan.

messages.text: We are getting close to the deadline for the Crisis Communication Playbook for On-site Security Incidents, so I would like to use this thread to check readiness for rollout and next steps.  Current status as I see it:  - A1 (Crisis Communication Playbook v1.0) skeleton is in place, with sections being filled based on T1–T9.  - A2 (On-Site Incident Escalation Checklist) is close to final pending any last feedback from guard testing.  - A3 and A5 (holding statements and multi-channel strategy) have agreed defaults and severity levels.  - A4, A6, and A7 (internal briefings, drill plan, and review procedure) are drafted and aligned.  Remaining work includes T10 (post-incident review process details) and T12 (final consolidation and distribution).  Let us confirm what is left to do, who owns it, and how we will distribute A1 and related materials to stakeholders.

From my side, the main remaining piece is to finalise A7 and T10: the post-incident review and improvement process. I have a draft that includes:  - A standard review template (what happened, what worked, what did not, what to change in A1–A6).  - Roles and timing: initial review within 72 hours, deeper review within two weeks for major incidents.  - A simple workflow for updating A1 and notifying stakeholders when changes are made.  I will circulate this draft today for quick comments. Once we agree, we can mark T10 as done and link A7 clearly from A1.

On training and internal briefings, A4 and A6 are ready for v1. I have incorporated the decisions from earlier threads and aligned the language with A3 and A5.  For rollout, I suggest we:  - Run at least one live 60-minute session per major site before the next quarterly safety drill, using A2, A4, and A6.  - Provide the recorded overview and templates to smaller sites that cannot host a full session immediately.  I can draft a short internal announcement that points staff to A1 and explains what to expect from the training.

We tested the A2 checklists for two scenarios with a small group of guards. Overall they found them clear and liked the See/Say/Send/Secure/Share pattern. The main feedback was to make the font a bit larger for printed versions and to keep the 'do not' list very short.  I have passed these comments to 286680, but from a guard point of view, I think A2 is ready to go for v1.
